title: O7 – Decision-making: rational model, Simon, Carnegie, Janis, Allison

blocks.text: The rational model (classical economics) assumes the decision maker knows and evaluates all alternatives and all consequences and picks the optimal one – an ideal, but a utopia.
Simon's bounded rationality is the “real world” model: limited information, cognition and time → managers satisfice (first satisfactory solution) and search sequentially, not synoptically.
Organisations are decision-support systems: division of labour, hierarchy, rules and information channels reduce complexity and absorb uncertainty.

Carnegie model (Cyert, March & Simon): organisational decisions come from coalitions with different interests; goals are negotiated compromises; the overall solution is a juxtaposition of local solutions.
Groups decide with more information and commitment but suffer from conformity, social loafing, polarisation and groupthink (Janis, 8 symptoms).
Allison analyses one decision through three lenses: bounded rationality (biases), organisational model (structure, culture, incentives) and political model (power games) – Cuban Missile Crisis 1962.

Comes from economics (classical theory: Adam Smith, Ricardo, Walras). The decision maker can identify and evaluate all possible alternatives and all their consequences and rationally chooses the most appropriate course of action → the decision is optimal (“no better”) (Jones & George, 2008).

Recognise the problem → identify the objectives → gather and evaluate data, diagnose (synoptic evaluation from one point of view) → list and evaluate all alternatives (each analysed independently, all consequences in time and space, then compared) → select the best course of action to optimise the firm's value system → implement → gather feedback → follow up.
An ideal managers strive for, but unrealistic: it ignores time constraints and the limits of human knowledge and information-processing capabilities.
Deciding costs effort – Barack Obama wore only grey or blue suits to avoid trivial daily decisions.
The environment is too complex for one person to understand and know.

Information is incomplete and imperfect · limited information-processing capacity and selective perception · too many alternatives to consider them all · impossible to foresee all consequences in time and space · limited time · preferences not clearly predefined.
“Optimisation” criteria are replaced by “satisfactory performance” criteria; the search is sequential (one option after another), not synoptic (all at once).
Managers choose the FIRST satisfactory and sufficient solution – not the optimal one – that respects the organisational status quo and can be taken quickly from incomplete information.

Jacques Chirac's dissolution of the National Assembly in 1997 (meant to strengthen his majority, it led to defeat and cohabitation with Lionel Jospin, 1997–2002); Daniel Kahneman: “We're blind to our blindness” – we have very little idea of how little we know.
Organisations help overcome bounded rationality and get closer to rational decisions: structure, procedures, rules, culture and incentives reduce complexity and absorb uncertainty.
Reduces each person's field of attention and competence to a manageable size.
Spares people from questioning whether orders are sound and releases them from responsibility (cf. Weber, Milgram's agentic state).
Ready-made solutions.
Those who collect information are not those who use it.
Researchers at Carnegie-Mellon University extended bounded rationality to the organisation: organisation-level decisions are based on coalitions among managers (Daft, 2009).
Large firms are coalitions of individuals or sub-groups (managers, stockholders, workers, suppliers …) with different interests; all take part in setting goals and making decisions.

Specific goals (production, inventory, market share, sales, profits) are compromises negotiated by the sub-groups; priorities and information vary by group → potential conflicts. All goals must be satisfied, following an implicit order of priority.
The problem is split into sub-problems (secondary goals) solved by sub-groups by specialty, each with its standard procedures, to satisfy its own hierarchy.
Once a solution satisfactory to the hierarchy is found, the process stops (satisficing, sequential). The overall solution is the simple juxtaposition of local solutions.

“Two heads are better than one” underpins democratic and judicial systems; selection committees, executive committees, parliaments, boards and juries decide as groups. Irving Janis studied their mechanisms and liabilities.

More complete information and knowledge · more diverse views and creativity by pooling resources · greater acceptance of and commitment to the decision (members had a voice) · synergy through mutual influence and better understanding of the decision.
Time-consuming · pressure to conform · discussion dominated by a few members, a clique or a forceful leader · ambiguous responsibility and social loafing (Ringelmann's rope pull, free riders).
All arguments must be based on facts; intimate conviction does not count in collective reasoning.
Warning signals are minimised so as not to be the messenger of bad news (pilots and control tower).
When members share a common normative orientation, persuasive arguments escalate and members adopt the group's prototypical opinion → the decision radicalises, groups can adopt extreme attitudes.
A group makes faulty decisions because of “a deterioration of mental efficiency, reality testing, and moral judgment resulting from pressure within the group”.

Illusion of invulnerability (excessive optimism, extreme risks) · collective rationalisation (warnings discounted) · belief in inherent morality (ethical consequences ignored) · stereotyped views of out-groups (negotiation seems unnecessary) · direct pressure on dissenters (loyalty = adopting the group view) · self-censorship (doubts not expressed) · illusion of unanimity (majority view taken as unanimous) · self-appointed “mindguards” (shield the group and leader from contradictory information).
Members with similar backgrounds · group insulated from outside opinions · no clear rules for decision-making.
Alternatives are ignored; irrational actions that dehumanise other groups.
Pearl Harbor, Bay of Pigs invasion, escalation of the Vietnam War, the Iran hostage rescue; later the invasion of Iraq (Bush administration and Congress).

sections.heading: Allison: three approaches to analyse decisions (1971)

blocks.text: The decision is made by individuals with limited resources, limited time and limited cognitive skills. Focus: biases.
The decision is shaped by organisational processes and features. Focus: structure, culture, incentives (Sessions 3–5).
The decision is the output of negotiation and interplay between actors with specific interests. Focus: power games (Session 6).
Allison, Essence of Decision (1971): the US response to Soviet missiles in Cuba explained with all three lenses – exercise in class: apply them yourself.
